headline: Kanzuru is 感 plus する, with suru voiced to zuru by rendaku.
Sei, “cause, reason, fault”, is probably a shift from shoi.
“To eat” began as the humble “to receive” 食ぶ (tabu), the humble form of 賜ぶ (tabu, “to (deign to) give”).
Massao is older 真青 (masao) with a doubled consonant for emphasis, first cited in the Nippo Jisho of 1603.
Kaneru is from Old Japanese 兼ぬ (kanu), from Proto-Japonic *kan-a-.
Sakarau, “to go against”, is built on 逆 (saka).
Rōdō is Middle Chinese 勞動, and 動 was replaced by the kokuji 働 from 1897, when the labour movement gained hold in Japan.
Kajitsu is from Middle Chinese 果實.
Nama, “raw”, is from Old Japanese, with numerous derivatives already in use in the Heian period.
Darashinai is from しだらない (shidaranai).
Yaku is from Middle Chinese 役, the goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
Kōhai is Middle Chinese 後輩, literally “back, behind” plus “people of a certain kind”, first cited to a text from 827 CE.
Asobi is the continuative stem of 遊ぶ (asobu).
Nareru is from Old Japanese 慣る (naru).
Joshu is simply described as “from Sinitic”.
Yōkyū is from Middle Chinese 要求 (MC 'jiew gjuw).
Sanka, “oxidation”, is 酸 (san) plus 化 (-ka, “-ization”), the same 酸 as in 酸素 (sanso), literally “acidic/sour element”.
Hatsu's kanji 発 is a shinjitai, simplified from 發.
Kan, “pipe”, is from Middle Chinese 管, and the pipe sense is traced back to the writings of Zhuangzi.
Higaeri is 日 (hi, “day”) plus 帰り (kaeri, “return”), with kaeri voiced to gaeri.
Gun, “group”, is from Middle Chinese 群.
Gasorin is from American English gasoline.
Uttaeru went from urutapu to uttafu to uttaheru to uttaeru, and is attested since at least the early Heian period.
Senmen is attested from the 13th century.
Yakuwari is 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) plus 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).
Moeru is from the classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu), by way of moju and mojeru.
Ōu is the Old Japanese verb 覆ふ (opu, “cover from above”) plus ふ (-fu), which expresses repetition or ongoing state.
Tō, “tower”, abbreviates 卒塔婆 (sotoba), a transliteration of Sanskrit stūpa, “heap”.
Su, “nest”, is found in the Kojiki of 712, from Proto-Japonic *su.
Chii is from Middle Chinese 地位, first cited in Japanese in the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing.
Sensu is first attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.
